title: Bowling Ball and Feather Drop
description: The vacuum-chamber demo, run in air. A 5 kg bowling ball and a 10 g feather are released together from 2 m, each drawn with three force arrows — weight (F_g), drag (F_d), and their sum (F_net). Both feel the same quadratic drag law, F = ½·ρ·Cd·A·|v|·v; the difference is entirely in how much that force matters against each body's weight. On the ball, the drag arrow stays a stub next to a 49 N weight: its terminal velocity is about 45 m/s, far beyond anything a 2 m drop can reach, so F_net holds steady at m·g and it lands at roughly 6.2 m/s after 0.63 s. On the feather, the drag arrow visibly grows until it exactly cancels the weight arrow and F_net vanishes — terminal velocity is about 1.6 m/s, reached in the first quarter of the fall, after which it drifts down at constant speed and lands around 1.3 s, roughly 0.7 s behind the ball. The vanishing F_net arrow IS the lesson: terminal velocity is not 'no gravity', it is gravity exactly cancelled. Read the acceleration graph alongside it — the ball sits pinned near −9.8 m/s² while the feather's climbs to zero. Diorama-scoped authoring notes: the feather is rotated 90° (ObjectConfig.angle is in RADIANS, unlike ramp and vector angles which follow env.angleUnit) so it falls flat-side-on, and because drag's default reference area is the authored WIDTH and is NOT rotation-aware, referenceArea is set explicitly to 0.1 m² so the modelled frontal area matches the area the picture shows. Both bodies carry real drag coefficients rather than the earlier Cd = 0 opt-out, and the feather carries a real 10 g mass rather than one dialed up for arrow visibility.
